views.name: sales_denorm
views.body_sql:
SELECT
  sales.prod_id AS prod_id,
  sales.cust_id AS cust_id,
  sales.time_id AS time_id,
  sales.channel_id AS channel_id,
  sales.promo_id AS promo_id,
  sales.quantity_sold AS quantity_sold,
  sales.amount_sold AS amount_sold,
  products.prod_name AS prod_name,
  products.prod_subcategory AS prod_subcategory,
  products.prod_subcategory_id AS prod_subcategory_id,
  products.prod_category AS prod_category,
  products.prod_category_id AS prod_category_id,
  products.supplier_id AS supplier_id,
  customers.cust_first_name AS cust_first_name,
  customers.cust_last_name AS cust_last_name,
  customers.cust_gender AS cust_gender,
  customers.cust_year_of_birth AS cust_year_of_birth,
  customers.cust_city AS cust_city,
  customers.country_id AS country_id,
  times.calendar_year AS calendar_year,
  times.calendar_month_desc AS calendar_month_desc,
  channels.channel_desc AS channel_desc,
  channels.channel_class AS channel_class,
  promotions.promo_name AS promo_name,
  promotions.promo_category AS promo_category,
  promotions.promo_subcategory AS promo_subcategory
FROM sales
LEFT JOIN products ON sales.prod_id = products.prod_id
LEFT JOIN customers ON sales.cust_id = customers.cust_id
LEFT JOIN times ON sales.time_id = times.time_id
LEFT JOIN channels ON sales.channel_id = channels.channel_id
LEFT JOIN promotions ON sales.promo_id = promotions.promo_id

params.description: A denormalized sales-level view that answers transactional questions at the grain of (prod_id, cust_id, time_id, channel_id, promo_id) showing sold quantity, sales amount and associated product, customer, time, channel and promotion attributes.
params.when_to_use: Drill into individual sales transactions or sales-level aggregates partitioned by product, customer, time period, channel or promotion. | Build aggregations (SUM/COUNT) after grouping at the same grain or a coarser grain (e.g., monthly product totals) — ensure you aggregate measures from this view, not join additional many-row tables first. | Filter by any product, customer, time, channel or promotion attribute while keeping correct transaction-level measures before aggregation.
params.when_not_to_use: Joining this view to other one-to-many child tables (e.g., multiple price records per product) without re-aggregating first — doing so will multiply sales rows and overstate measures. | Using this view to produce pre-aggregated metrics (e.g., monthly totals) without applying an explicit aggregation like SUM(amount_sold) grouped by the desired coarser grain — the view is transactional, not pre-rolled. | Attempting to compute per-customer lifetime metrics by simply DISTINCT-ing cust_id here — duplicate prod/time/channel/promo combinations can exist and require proper aggregation (SUM/COUNT) to produce correct lifetime totals. | Joining on non-key columns (e.g., product name) to bring in other datasets — this can convert intended one-to-one joins into many-to-many matches and silently inflate or deflate measures.
params.output_schema: prod_id: product identifier from sales.prod_id (base sales table key) | cust_id: customer identifier from sales.cust_id (base sales table key) | time_id: time identifier from sales.time_id (base sales table key) | channel_id: channel identifier from sales.channel_id (base sales table key) | promo_id: promotion identifier from sales.promo_id (base sales table key) | quantity_sold: sold quantity for the sales row from sales.quantity_sold (transaction-level metric, numeric) | amount_sold: sales amount for the sales row from sales.amount_sold (transaction-level metric, numeric) | prod_name: product name attribute from products.prod_name (dimension attribute joined by prod_id) | prod_subcategory: product subcategory name from products.prod_subcategory (dimension attribute) | prod_subcategory_id: product subcategory identifier from products.prod_subcategory_id (dimension attribute) | prod_category: product category name from products.prod_category (dimension attribute) | prod_category_id: product category identifier from products.prod_category_id (dimension attribute) | supplier_id: supplier identifier from products.supplier_id (dimension attribute) | cust_first_name: customer first name from customers.cust_first_name (dimension attribute) | cust_last_name: customer last name from customers.cust_last_name (dimension attribute) | cust_gender: customer gender from customers.cust_gender (dimension attribute) | cust_year_of_birth: customer year of birth from customers.cust_year_of_birth (dimension attribute) | cust_city: customer city from customers.cust_city (dimension attribute) | country_id: customer country identifier from customers.country_id (dimension attribute) | calendar_year: year label from times.calendar_year (time dimension attribute) | calendar_month_desc: month description from times.calendar_month_desc (time dimension attribute) | channel_desc: channel description from channels.channel_desc (channel dimension attribute) | channel_class: channel class from channels.channel_class (channel dimension attribute) | promo_name: promotion name from promotions.promo_name (promotion dimension attribute) | promo_category: promotion category from promotions.promo_category (promotion dimension attribute) | promo_subcategory: promotion subcategory from promotions.promo_subcategory (promotion dimension attribute)
params.grounded_columns: sales.prod_id | sales.cust_id | sales.time_id | sales.channel_id | sales.promo_id | sales.quantity_sold | sales.amount_sold | products.prod_name | products.prod_subcategory | products.prod_subcategory_id | products.prod_category | products.prod_category_id | products.supplier_id | customers.cust_first_name | customers.cust_last_name | customers.cust_gender | customers.cust_year_of_birth | customers.cust_city | customers.country_id | times.calendar_year | times.calendar_month_desc | channels.channel_desc | channels.channel_class | promotions.promo_name | promotions.promo_category | promotions.promo_subcategory
params.metric: quantity_sold = direct transactional column sales.quantity_sold (do not SUM unless aggregating to coarser grain) | amount_sold = direct transactional column sales.amount_sold (do not SUM unless aggregating to coarser grain)
params.composition: Cardinality-SAFE: join to product-level or product-dimension views/tables on products.prod_id = prod_id — products is expected to be one-row-per-prod_id so this will NOT duplicate sales measures. | Cardinality-SAFE: join to customers dimension on customers.cust_id = cust_id — customers is expected to be one-row-per-cust_id so sales measures are preserved. | Cardinality-SAFE: join to times dimension on times.time_id = time_id — times is one-row-per-time_id so measures are preserved. | Cardinality-SAFE: join to channels on channels.channel_id = channel_id — channels is one-row-per-channel_id so measures are preserved. | Cardinality-SAFE: join to promotions on promotions.promo_id = promo_id — promotions is one-row-per-promo_id so measures are preserved. | Do NOT join to product_price_cost (AGG) or customer_lifetime_sales (AGG) directly without aligning grains — those are aggregated objects and may be at a different grain; joining can double-count unless you aggregate this view to the same grain first. | Do NOT join to product_rank_within_month (RANK) without ensuring uniqueness per (prod_id, time_id) — if that sibling has multiple rows per sales grain it will multiply rows and measures. | If you must enrich with any one-to-many datasets (for example, multiple price rows per prod_id or multiple loyalty-events per cust_id), first aggregate those datasets to one-row-per-join-key (e.g., latest price per prod_id or summed events per cust_id) and then join to this view to avoid multiplying sales measures.
params.comparison: use product_price_cost (AGG) instead when you need pre-aggregated price or cost metrics at product-level — that view already contains aggregated price/cost measures and avoids aggregating this transactional view upward yourself. | use monthly_sales_by_product (AGG) instead when you only need monthly rollups by product — it returns pre-aggregated monthly totals so you don't need to SUM(amount_sold) from this transactional view. | use customer_demographics (JOIN) when you only need customer attributes without transactional measures — customer_demographics focuses on customer attributes and avoids joining the sales facts. | use product_rank_within_month (RANK) when you need rank-based metrics per product / month — it includes ranking logic and possibly different deduplication rules than the raw transaction-level data. | use customer_lifetime_sales (AGG) when you need pre-computed lifetime metrics per customer — this sibling produces aggregated lifetime totals and handles deduplication/aggregation for you. | use fx_monthly (NORM) when you need normalized monthly foreign-exchange adjustments applied to aggregated amounts — fx_monthly is designed to be joined at the monthly currency/time grain and may require aligning this view's time aggregation before applying FX.

views.description: Denormalized sales transactions joined to core dimensions (products, customers, times, channels, promotions). Use this when analyzing transactions with descriptive attributes from dimensions or when building further aggregates. | Use for: Transaction-level reporting combining product/customer/time/channel/promo attributes; Drilldowns from aggregated metrics to underlying transactions; Filtering transactions by product category, customer demographics, time period, channel or promotion

views.name: product_price_cost
views.body_sql:
SELECT
  prod_id AS prod_id,
  time_id AS time_id,
  promo_id AS promo_id,
  channel_id AS channel_id,
  AVG(unit_cost) AS avg_unit_cost,
  AVG(unit_price) AS avg_unit_price,
  MIN(unit_cost) AS min_unit_cost,
  MAX(unit_cost) AS max_unit_cost,
  COUNT(*) AS records_in_costs
FROM costs
GROUP BY
  prod_id,
  time_id,
  promo_id,
  channel_id

params.description: Per-product / per-time / per-promo / per-channel aggregated unit cost and price statistics (avg/min/max) computed from the costs table.
params.when_to_use: Calculate average unit cost or price for a specific product within a specific time period, promotion, and channel. | Compare min/max unit cost for a product by promo and channel in a given time bucket. | Filter or segment performance by prod_id × time_id × promo_id × channel_id and use the aggregated cost/price metrics directly.
params.when_not_to_use: Joining this view to a table that is many-to-one back to costs (for example a raw transactions table with multiple cost rows per transaction) without re-aggregation — this will multiply counts and averages and produce silently wrong measures because the view is at prod_id×time_id×promo_id×channel_id grain while the other side may be more granular. | Using this view to measure customer-level or transaction-level metrics (e.g., revenue per customer or per-order) — those require a different grain and will mis-count if you treat these aggregates as raw-level rows. | Attempting to compute time series trends at a finer time grain than time_id (e.g., daily when time_id is monthly) — mixing grains without correct rollup or disaggregation yields incorrect averages/counts. | Joining directly to any one-to-many dimension (e.g., a table of multiple SKUs per product variant or many channel_subtypes per channel) without first reducing the dimension to one row per channel_id, because that will duplicate rows and distort aggregated measures.
params.output_schema: prod_id: product identifier — sourced from costs.prod_id (grouping key) | time_id: time bucket identifier — sourced from costs.time_id (grouping key) | promo_id: promotion identifier — sourced from costs.promo_id (grouping key) | channel_id: channel identifier — sourced from costs.channel_id (grouping key) | avg_unit_cost: average of unit_cost within the group — derived as AVG(costs.unit_cost) | avg_unit_price: average of unit_price within the group — derived as AVG(costs.unit_price) | min_unit_cost: minimum unit_cost within the group — derived as MIN(costs.unit_cost) | max_unit_cost: maximum unit_cost within the group — derived as MAX(costs.unit_cost) | records_in_costs: count of source rows aggregated — derived as COUNT(*) on costs rows per group
params.grounded_columns: costs.prod_id | costs.time_id | costs.promo_id | costs.channel_id | costs.unit_cost | costs.unit_price
params.metric: avg_unit_cost = AVG(costs.unit_cost) | avg_unit_price = AVG(costs.unit_price) | min_unit_cost = MIN(costs.unit_cost) | max_unit_cost = MAX(costs.unit_cost) | records_in_costs = COUNT(*)
params.composition: cardinality-SAFE join guidance: join to product-level dimension (e.g., a product master view keyed by prod_id) on prod_id — safe because product master is one-row-per-prod_id, so it will not duplicate this view's rows or measures. | cardinality-SAFE join guidance: join to a time dimension (e.g., calendar/time lookup) on time_id — safe because time dimension is one-row-per-time_id. | cardinality-SAFE join guidance: join to a promotions dimension on promo_id — safe if promotions is one-row-per-promo_id. | cardinality-SAFE join guidance: join to a channel dimension on channel_id — safe if channel dimension is one-row-per-channel_id. | do NOT join to sales_denorm (JOIN) or any other join/multi-row-per-key table on prod_id/time_id/promo_id/channel_id without first aggregating that table to the same grain, because those sources may contain multiple sales rows per cost-group and will multiply this view's aggregated measures leading to inflated counts and incorrect averages. | do NOT join directly to customer_demographics or other customer-level tables on non-matching keys (e.g., customer_id) — these are different grains and will require explicit aggregation/rollup or summary tables to avoid duplication. | when combining measures: if you need to sum or average across larger grouping keys (for example, sum of records_in_costs across channels), aggregate this view's output (e.g., SUM(records_in_costs) GROUP BY prod_id,time_id,promo_id) rather than joining then aggregating the other table first, to avoid double-counting.
params.comparison: use monthly_sales_by_product instead when you need aggregated sales revenue/volume metrics rather than cost/price statistics — monthly_sales_by_product is focused on sales metrics and may have a different grain or join logic. | use sales_denorm when you need row-level sales transactions and to compute metrics that require transaction-level detail (joins to costs should be done carefully to avoid many-to-many multiplication). | use product_rank_within_month when you need ranking of products within a month; that view provides rank logic and likely uses sales measures rather than cost aggregates. | use customer_lifetime_sales when analysis is at the customer lifetime grain — it aggregates per-customer over time and is not substitute for per-product/per-time/promo/channel cost stats. | use fx_monthly when you need normalized foreign-exchange converted metrics across months; fx_monthly provides currency normalization which this view does not handle.

views.description: Per-product per-time pricing and cost summary from costs table exposing average unit_cost and unit_price and counts of records. Use for margin analysis or joining with sales aggregates. | Use for: Compute average cost/price per product and time period; Join unit cost/price to sales to compute margin; Identify periods or channels with missing or sparse cost records

views.name: monthly_sales_by_product
views.body_sql:
SELECT
  s.prod_id AS prod_id,
  t.calendar_year AS calendar_year,
  t.calendar_month_desc AS calendar_month_desc,
  SUM(s.quantity_sold) AS total_quantity_sold,
  SUM(s.amount_sold) AS total_amount_sold,
  COUNT(*) AS sales_row_count
FROM sales s
JOIN times t ON s.time_id = t.time_id
GROUP BY
  s.prod_id,
  t.calendar_year,
  t.calendar_month_desc

params.description: Monthly aggregated sales totals and row counts per product (product × calendar month-year).
params.when_to_use: Ask for product-level sales activity in a specific calendar month/year (e.g., "How many units and amount sold of product X in Mar 2024?"). | Build time-series charts of product monthly sales (units or amount) where each point is product × month. | Compare quantities or amounts across products for the same calendar month.
params.when_not_to_use: Do not use when you need transaction-level detail (e.g., individual sale timestamps or sale-level attributes) — this view is aggregated and loses row-level identifiers; using it for row-level joins will produce incorrect duplicates or loss of detail. | Do not use when the target grain is different (e.g., daily, weekly, customer × month, or product × year) — aggregations are at product × calendar_year × calendar_month_desc; using it to represent other grains without correct re-aggregation or repartitioning will silently miscount. | Do not join this view directly to one-to-many child tables (for example a table of multiple promotions per month or multiple customers per product-month) without re-aggregating the child side first — joining to one-to-many sides will multiply totals (double-counting of total_quantity_sold/total_amount_sold). | Do not use for currency conversion or FX adjustments — amounts are raw from sales.amount_sold; applying FX without aligning month keys and re-aggregation may be incorrect.
params.output_schema: prod_id: product identifier; derived from sales.prod_id (s.prod_id) — the dimension key at which aggregation is performed. | calendar_year: calendar year label for the aggregated time bucket; derived from times.calendar_year (t.calendar_year). | calendar_month_desc: human-readable month descriptor (e.g., 'Mar 2024'); derived from times.calendar_month_desc (t.calendar_month_desc). | total_quantity_sold: SUM(s.quantity_sold) over all sales rows for the given prod_id × calendar_month; source column: sales.quantity_sold aggregated by SUM. | total_amount_sold: SUM(s.amount_sold) over all sales rows for the given prod_id × calendar_month; source column: sales.amount_sold aggregated by SUM. | sales_row_count: COUNT(*) number of sales table rows aggregated into this product × month bucket; equals COUNT(*) from the joined sales×times rows for that group.
params.grounded_columns: sales.prod_id | sales.quantity_sold | sales.amount_sold | sales.time_id | times.time_id | times.calendar_year | times.calendar_month_desc
params.metric: total_quantity_sold = SUM(sales.quantity_sold)  -- aggregate at (prod_id, calendar_year, calendar_month_desc) | total_amount_sold = SUM(sales.amount_sold)      -- aggregate at (prod_id, calendar_year, calendar_month_desc) | sales_row_count = COUNT(*)                       -- count of sales rows contributing to the aggregate group
params.composition: Safe to join: join to a product dimension (product table/view) on prod_id — safe because product is one row per prod_id, so this view's aggregated measures will not be duplicated. | Safe to join: join to a month/time dimension (times or calendar lookup) on (calendar_year, calendar_month_desc) or on time_id after expanding to the same month grain — safe when the join preserves the one-row-per-month mapping. | Unsafe to join without care: do NOT join directly to transaction-level sales again (or any table that has multiple rows per prod_id × month) because that will multiply this view's aggregated measures (double counting). If you must combine with a one-to-many detail, perform aggregation on the detail to the same grain first and then join. | Unsafe to join without care: do NOT join to tables with multiple customer rows per product-month (for example a customer_orders table or promotions table with multiple rows per product-month) unless those tables are pre-aggregated to prod_id × calendar_month (or otherwise deduplicated). | Guidance: when combining metrics from another aggregated view, ensure both views share the exact same grain (prod_id, calendar_year, calendar_month_desc). If they do not, re-aggregate the finer-grained view to this view's grain before summing or averaging metrics.
params.comparison: use sales_denorm instead when you need row-level sales attributes or to perform additional joins at the sale-level — sales_denorm is a JOIN (non-aggregated) sibling that preserves transaction rows. | use product_price_cost instead when you need aggregated pricing/cost metrics (e.g., average price or cost per product-month) — that view is an AGG tailored to price/cost metrics while monthly_sales_by_product provides quantity and amount sums. | use product_rank_within_month instead when you need ranking of products within a month (e.g., top N by sales) — that RANK sibling computes rank metadata which this aggregated view does not. | use customer_lifetime_sales when the analysis is customer-centric (lifetime totals per customer) rather than product × month — it has a different grain (customer-level) and will not match this view's product-month grain. | use fx_monthly when you need normalized/FX-adjusted monetary amounts by month — fx_monthly provides currency normalization; if you join it to this view to convert total_amount_sold you must align on the same calendar month keys and re-compute amounts (do not naively multiply without ensuring one-to-one month mapping).

views.description: Monthly aggregated sales measures per product (calendar month), exposing quantity and amount totals. Use for trend analysis, product ranking, and month-over-month calculations. | Use for: Monthly product sales trends; Top products by month (can be combined with a ranking CTE); Month-over-month growth or comparisons

views.name: customer_demographics
views.body_sql:
SELECT
  customers.cust_id AS cust_id,
  customers.cust_first_name AS cust_first_name,
  customers.cust_last_name AS cust_last_name,
  customers.cust_gender AS cust_gender,
  customers.cust_year_of_birth AS cust_year_of_birth,
  customers.cust_marital_status AS cust_marital_status,
  customers.cust_city AS cust_city,
  customers.cust_state_province AS cust_state_province,
  customers.country_id AS country_id,
  supplementary_demographics.education AS education,
  supplementary_demographics.occupation AS occupation,
  supplementary_demographics.household_size AS household_size,
  supplementary_demographics.yrs_residence AS yrs_residence,
  supplementary_demographics.affinity_card AS affinity_card,
  supplementary_demographics.cricket AS cricket,
  supplementary_demographics.baseball AS baseball,
  supplementary_demographics.tennis AS tennis,
  supplementary_demographics.soccer AS soccer,
  supplementary_demographics.golf AS golf,
  supplementary_demographics.unknown AS unknown,
  supplementary_demographics.misc AS misc
FROM customers
LEFT JOIN supplementary_demographics ON customers.cust_id = supplementary_demographics.cust_id

params.description: One-row-per-customer demographic snapshot combining core customer identity with optional supplementary demographic attributes.
params.when_to_use: Lookup demographic attributes for an individual customer by cust_id (e.g., display name, city, gender, education). | Enrich event-level or transaction-level data with customer-level demographic attributes when joining on cust_id (ensuring you join in a way that preserves cardinality). | Build customer-segment lists or filters based on demographic fields (age cohort via cust_year_of_birth, marital status, household_size, affinities).
params.when_not_to_use: Do not use this view to compute aggregated customer metrics (counts, sums, averages) without first grouping by cust_id — aggregating incorrectly at a lower grain will produce mis-counts because the view is already one row per cust_id and must be the aggregation grain. | Do not join this view directly to one-to-many tables (for example, orders or transactions) expecting the view to remain at customer-grain; naive join will duplicate customer rows and will multiply any measures added afterwards (grain-mismatch). Instead aggregate the one-to-many side to cust_id first or use DISTINCT cust_id keys. | Do not use this view as a source of time-series metrics (cohort retention, monthly spend) — it contains static demographic attributes only and no temporal measures; using it without joining to time-aware, aggregated sales tables will produce misleading results.
params.output_schema: cust_id: Unique customer identifier — sourced from customers.cust_id. This is the grain of the view (one row per cust_id). | cust_first_name: Customer's first name — sourced from customers.cust_first_name. | cust_last_name: Customer's last name — Customer's last name — sourced from customers.cust_last_name. | cust_gender: Customer gender code or label — sourced from customers.cust_gender. | cust_year_of_birth: Year of birth (integer) — sourced from customers.cust_year_of_birth. | cust_marital_status: Marital status label/code — sourced from customers.cust_marital_status. | cust_city: City name from customer's address — sourced from customers.cust_city. | cust_state_province: State or province — sourced from customers.cust_state_province. | country_id: Country identifier for the customer — sourced from customers.country_id. | education: Education level from supplementary demographics — sourced from supplementary_demographics.education. | occupation: Occupation from supplementary demographics — sourced from supplementary_demographics.occupation. | household_size: Number of people in household (from supplementary data) — sourced from supplementary_demographics.household_size. | yrs_residence: Years at current residence — sourced from supplementary_demographics.yrs_residence. | affinity_card: Affinity card flag/label — sourced from supplementary_demographics.affinity_card. | cricket: Affinity boolean/score for cricket — sourced from supplementary_demographics.cricket. | baseball: Affinity boolean/score for baseball — sourced from supplementary_demographics.baseball. | tennis: Affinity boolean/score for tennis — sourced from supplementary_demographics.tennis. | soccer: Affinity boolean/score for soccer — sourced from supplementary_demographics.soccer. | golf: Affinity boolean/score for golf — sourced from supplementary_demographics.golf. | unknown: Affinity 'unknown' indicator from supplementary_demographics.unknown. | misc: Miscellaneous demographic flag/value — sourced from supplementary_demographics.misc.
params.grounded_columns: customers.cust_id | customers.cust_first_name | customers.cust_last_name | customers.cust_gender | customers.cust_year_of_birth | customers.cust_marital_status | customers.cust_city | customers.cust_state_province | customers.country_id | supplementary_demographics.cust_id | supplementary_demographics.education | supplementary_demographics.occupation | supplementary_demographics.household_size | supplementary_demographics.yrs_residence | supplementary_demographics.affinity_card | supplementary_demographics.cricket | supplementary_demographics.baseball | supplementary_demographics.tennis | supplementary_demographics.soccer | supplementary_demographics.golf | supplementary_demographics.unknown | supplementary_demographics.misc
params.metric: This view contains no derived aggregate metrics; all output columns are direct column projections. Example metric definitions (none are defined in SQL): | N/A = No aggregated measures in this view. If you need counts or sums, compute them by aggregating at cust_id or by joining to an aggregated sibling view (e.g., customer_lifetime_sales) rather than adding aggregation here.
params.composition: cardinality-SAFE join guidance: join to customer-level dimension or lookup tables on cust_id (for example, other one-row-per-customer tables) — safe because this view is one-row-per-cust_id and such joins will preserve one row per customer and will not duplicate its attributes. | Do NOT join directly to one-to-many tables (e.g., orders, transactions, sales_denorm which is likely one-to-many per customer) without aggregation. Example unsafe pattern: SELECT ... FROM customer_demographics cd JOIN orders o ON cd.cust_id = o.cust_id — this duplicates the customer row for each order and will multiply any metrics derived after the join. | If you need to combine with a one-to-many sibling (sales_denorm, monthly_sales_by_product, customer_lifetime_sales), first aggregate the one-to-many side to cust_id (e.g., SUM(amount) GROUP BY cust_id) or use a distinct key subquery, then join the aggregated result to this view on cust_id to avoid row multiplication. | Joining to dimensional attributes that are guaranteed one-to-one with cust_id (for example, a 'customer_status' table keyed by cust_id) is safe without re-aggregation because there is no duplication. | This view uses LEFT JOIN to supplementary_demographics, so missing supplementary rows will result in NULLs — be explicit in downstream logic to treat NULLs appropriately (e.g., COALESCE or separate 'unknown' bucket) to avoid silently treating absent data as a valid category.
params.comparison: use customer_lifetime_sales instead when you need aggregated monetary metrics per customer (this sibling is an AGG that contains lifetime sums/counts) — customer_demographics has identity and demographic attributes only. | use sales_denorm instead when you need transaction-level or order-level detail; sales_denorm is JOIN-based and contains one row per transaction/sale whereas customer_demographics is one row per customer. | use monthly_sales_by_product or product_rank_within_month when you need time-bucketed product performance or ranks — these are aggregated/time-aware views and not appropriate for static customer attributes. | use product_price_cost when you need product-level aggregated price/cost metrics — unrelated grain and purpose. | use fx_monthly when you need currency normalization over time — customer_demographics is not time- or FX-aware.

views.description: Customer records joined with supplementary demographics and country attributes. Use for customer segmentation and demographic-based analyses. | Use for: Customer segmentation by demographics and sports affinities; Joining customer demographics to sales for RFM or lifetime value analyses; Filtering customers by demographic attributes

views.name: product_rank_within_month
views.body_sql:
SELECT
  m.prod_id AS prod_id,
  m.calendar_year AS calendar_year,
  m.calendar_month_desc AS calendar_month_desc,
  m.total_amount_sold AS total_amount_sold,
  RANK() OVER (PARTITION BY m.calendar_year, m.calendar_month_desc ORDER BY m.total_amount_sold DESC) AS month_amount_rank
FROM monthly_sales_by_product m

params.description: Ranks products by total amount sold within each calendar month and year, returning the product monthly sales and its rank within that month.
params.when_to_use: You want the position (rank) of each product by dollars sold within a specific calendar month (e.g., top N products in a month). | You need to display product monthly revenue and compare relative performance of products inside the same month (month-over-month ranking comparisons). | Filtering to a single calendar_year and calendar_month_desc to show month leaderboards or to join to a month-level report where one row per product per month is appropriate.
params.when_not_to_use: Joining row-level transactional data (e.g., orders/line_items) directly to this view to compute sums — doing so can double-count because this view is already aggregated to product × month. | Using this view to compute customer- or order-level metrics (cohort or retention) — the grain is product × month, not customer or order, so user-level analyses would be incorrect. | Treating the rank as comparable across different partitioning schemes (e.g., ranking across a year or across regions) — the rank is computed per calendar_year + calendar_month_desc and will be silently wrong if you expect a different partition. | Joining a one-to-many child (for example product_reviews or product_variants without re-aggregation) without first collapsing that child to product × month — that would multiply rows and distort total_amount_sold and ranks.
params.output_schema: prod_id: product identifier — derived from monthly_sales_by_product.prod_id | calendar_year: calendar year for the metric — derived from monthly_sales_by_product.calendar_year | calendar_month_desc: human-friendly month description (e.g., '2024-06') — derived from monthly_sales_by_product.calendar_month_desc | total_amount_sold: total sales amount for the product during the given month — sourced from monthly_sales_by_product.total_amount_sold (an aggregate metric in that base view) | month_amount_rank: rank of the product within that calendar month by total_amount_sold, 1 = highest amount — computed as RANK() OVER (PARTITION BY calendar_year, calendar_month_desc ORDER BY total_amount_sold DESC)
params.metric: total_amount_sold = monthly_sales_by_product.total_amount_sold  -- pre-aggregated sum of amount sold for prod_id in that calendar_year × calendar_month_desc | month_amount_rank = RANK() OVER (PARTITION BY monthly_sales_by_product.calendar_year, monthly_sales_by_product.calendar_month_desc ORDER BY monthly_sales_by_product.total_amount_sold DESC)  -- ordinal rank, ties produce same rank and gaps
params.composition: cardinality-SAFE join guidance: join to product-level dimension views (e.g., product_price_cost) on prod_id — safe because product_price_cost should be one row per prod_id (or aggregated to one row) so it will not duplicate monthly_sales_by_product rows or its measures. | cardinality-SAFE join guidance: join to month-level or calendar dimension on (calendar_year, calendar_month_desc) — safe because calendar dimensions are one row per month and will not duplicate measures. | do NOT join to one-to-many tables/views such as sales_denorm (a JOINed row-level table) or customer_demographics (if many customers map to a product) without first aggregating them to prod_id × calendar_year × calendar_month_desc. Joining directly to these will multiply rows and inflate/duplicate total_amount_sold and break ranking. | do NOT join to product_variants, product_images, reviews, or other multi-row product children on prod_id directly — either aggregate those to one row per prod_id (or per prod_id × month) before joining, or join using EXISTS/ARRAYS to avoid row multiplication. | If you need to combine with customer_lifetime_sales or fx_monthly, ensure you aggregate or normalize them to the same grain (prod_id × calendar_year × calendar_month_desc) or join only on the month keys (for fx_monthly) where fx_monthly is one row per month so measures are not duplicated.
params.comparison: use monthly_sales_by_product instead when you only need raw monthly metrics (total_amount_sold) and not the rank — monthly_sales_by_product provides the underlying aggregated measures and possibly additional metrics. | use sales_denorm when you need row-level transactional detail or to recompute different aggregations or filters before aggregating — sales_denorm is appropriate for building new aggregates at different grains. | use product_price_cost when you need product pricing or cost attributes (per-product dimensions) — product_price_cost is a sibling that holds product-level attributes and should be joined in (one-to-one) when enriching this view. | use customer_lifetime_sales when the analysis target is customer lifetime metrics; that view is at a different grain (customer) and should not replace this product × month ranking view.

views.description: Per-month rank of products by total_amount_sold, exposing rank and total_amount_sold. Useful for top-N product queries per month when combined with a rank filter. | Use for: Top-N products by revenue within each month; Temporal ranking of products to find movers and shakers; Combining ranks with product attributes to profile top performers

views.name: customer_lifetime_sales
views.body_sql:
SELECT
  s.cust_id AS cust_id,
  COUNT(*) AS purchase_count,
  SUM(s.quantity_sold) AS lifetime_quantity_sold,
  SUM(s.amount_sold) AS lifetime_amount_sold,
  MIN(s.time_id) AS first_purchase_date,
  MAX(s.time_id) AS last_purchase_date
FROM sales s
GROUP BY s.cust_id

params.description: Per-customer lifetime sales aggregates: count of purchase events, sum of quantity and amount, and first/last purchase dates.
params.when_to_use: To get a single-row-per-customer summary of total purchases and amounts across all time (customer lifetime metrics). | As the customer-level input when you need lifetime totals for joining to customer attributes or for per-customer reporting. | When computing customer-level retention, CLV-style inputs, simple segments by lifetime spend or purchase frequency.
params.when_not_to_use: Joining directly to transaction-level or other one-to-many detail tables without re-aggregation — doing so will duplicate the per-customer aggregates (grain mismatch). | Using it to compute time-windowed cohorts (e.g., first 90-day spend after acquisition) — this view is aggregated across all time and loses event-level timing/cohort boundaries. | Joining to tables that add extra rows per customer (for example monthly_sales_by_product or product_rank_within_month) without pre-aggregating those tables back to one row per customer — that will multiply purchase_count and sums. | Using purchase_count as a distinct customer count metric — purchase_count here is count of sales rows per customer (events), not count of customers.
params.output_schema: cust_id: The customer identifier (s.cust_id) — the grouping key; one row per cust_id. | purchase_count: Number of sales rows for this customer (COUNT(*) over sales rows). Source: COUNT(*) computed from sales table aliased s. | lifetime_quantity_sold: Sum of sales.quantity_sold for this customer (SUM(s.quantity_sold)). | lifetime_amount_sold: Sum of sales.amount_sold for this customer (SUM(s.amount_sold)). | first_purchase_date: Earliest sales.time_id for this customer (MIN(s.time_id)) — represents the timestamp/date of first recorded sale in sales table. | last_purchase_date: Latest sales.time_id for this customer (MAX(s.time_id)) — represents the timestamp/date of most recent recorded sale in sales table.
params.metric: purchase_count = COUNT(*) -- count of sales rows grouped by sales.cust_id | lifetime_quantity_sold = SUM(sales.quantity_sold) -- total quantity sold to the customer | lifetime_amount_sold = SUM(sales.amount_sold) -- total revenue/amount from the customer | first_purchase_date = MIN(sales.time_id) -- earliest time_id for the customer's sales rows | last_purchase_date = MAX(sales.time_id) -- latest time_id for the customer's sales rows
params.composition: Cardinality-SAFE: join to customer_demographics on customer_lifetime_sales.cust_id = customer_demographics.cust_id — safe because both are one-row-per-customer (this view is aggregated to one row per cust_id), so aggregates are not duplicated. | Cardinality-SAFE: join to product_price_cost only if that view is one-row-per-product AND you join via a product key that does not expand customers; if joining product-level data directly to customers, ensure the join key is truly one-to-one for the intended analysis. | Do NOT join directly to sales (transaction-level) on cust_id without re-aggregating sales first — joining back to sales will produce one row per sale and will duplicate the customer-level aggregates (multiplying purchase_count, sums). Instead, either: |   - join this view to customer_demographics (one-to-one) for enriched customer attributes, or |   - join to a pre-aggregated, one-row-per-customer-from-X view, or |   - if you must combine with transaction detail, join at the transaction level and then re-derive customer aggregates from transactions (do not reuse these aggregates across duplicated rows). | Do NOT join to monthly_sales_by_product or product_rank_within_month without reducing those to one row per customer (they are monthly/product-level and will create many rows per customer), because that will multiply this view's measures and produce incorrect totals.
params.comparison: Use sales_denorm instead when you need transaction-level detail (timestamps, product ids per sale) or to compute time-windowed metrics — sales_denorm is a JOIN and keeps row-level granularity. | Use monthly_sales_by_product instead when you need time-bucketed (monthly) aggregates by product — it provides monthly/product grain rather than customer lifetime grain. | Use product_price_cost when you need product-level cost/price aggregates — it is at product grain and contains economics per product rather than per-customer lifetime totals. | Use customer_demographics when you need customer attributes (age, segment, acquisition channel) — that view is suitable to enrich this view but not to replace these lifetime aggregates. | Do not substitute product_rank_within_month for customer_lifetime_sales — it is a ranked product/month view and does not provide customer-level lifetime sums. | Use fx_monthly when you need currency normalization across months — if sales.amount_sold requires FX conversion, convert amounts before aggregating to customer lifetime or re-aggregate using normalized amounts (fx_monthly is monthly-normalization and not directly comparable without aligning time grain).

views.description: Lifetime aggregated sales per customer exposing total quantity and amount purchased and first/last purchase dates. Useful for LTV, retention and cohort analysis. | Use for: Customer lifetime value and recency/frequency analysis; Segmenting customers by purchase activity and recency; Identifying churned vs active customers by last_purchase_date

views.name: fx_monthly
views.body_sql:
SELECT
  year AS year,
  month AS month,
  to_us AS to_us,
  printf('%04d-%02d', year, month) AS year_month
FROM currency

params.description: Provides monthly currency conversion/lookup rows: one row per year+month with the conversion value to USD (to_us) and a formatted year-month string.
params.when_to_use: Look up the currency conversion value for a specific year and month (e.g., join a month key to get the to_us rate). | Build time-series outputs at a year+month grain where each month should appear exactly once. | Labeling or grouping by formatted month (year_month) when the grouping key is year+month.
params.when_not_to_use: Joining directly to transactional/detail tables without ensuring those tables are one-row-per-month: doing so will multiply rows and effectively repeat the to_us value for each joined detail row (grain mismatch). | Using this view as if it were an aggregated measure across other dimensions (product/customer): it is not pre-aggregated over those dimensions and will lead to incorrect counts/sums if you expect per-product or per-customer uniqueness. | Using year_month alone as a cohort/cohort-aggregation key when transactions carry a day or other finer grain without first aggregating transactions to the year+month grain — this causes mis-counting or duplicated measures.
params.output_schema: year: calendar year integer; sourced from currency.year | month: calendar month integer (1-12); sourced from currency.month | to_us: conversion/value field representing 'to_us'; sourced from currency.to_us | year_month: string formatted as 'YYYY-MM' built from currency.year and currency.month via printf('%04d-%02d', year, month)
params.metric: to_us = currency.to_us (no aggregation; passed through from base table) | year_month = printf('%04d-%02d', currency.year, currency.month) (expression combining two base columns)
params.composition: Safe: join to calendar/month-dimension on (year, month) — this view is one-row-per (year,month) so joining on those keys will not duplicate to_us. | Safe: join to other one-row-per-month summary views (e.g., another monthly-aggregated view) on (year, month) — cardinality-preserving because both sides are at the same grain. | Do NOT join directly to transactional/detail tables (orders, line_items, sales transactions) on (year, month) unless you first aggregate those detail tables to one-row-per (year,month). Direct join would repeat the same to_us value for every matching transaction row and therefore multiply any measures derived from to_us. | Do NOT join to any child table that is one-to-many with respect to (year, month) (for example product-level rows within a month) without re-aggregation on that child side — otherwise the per-month to_us value becomes duplicated across the many side.
params.comparison: use sales_denorm instead when you need transactional sales rows joined with currency and product/customer details — sales_denorm is a JOIN-style denormalized view suited for row-level analysis, whereas fx_monthly is strictly monthly currency data. | use product_price_cost when you need aggregated price/cost metrics per product (AGG) — that sibling aggregates across product dimensions, whereas fx_monthly only provides month-level currency values. | use monthly_sales_by_product when you require per-product monthly sales aggregates — monthly_sales_by_product shares the (year,month) grain but includes product-level aggregation needed for per-product metrics. | use product_rank_within_month when you need ranks within each month — that view contains ranking logic per product/month; fx_monthly only supplies the currency rate per month. | use customer_lifetime_sales when analysing customer lifetime aggregates — that view aggregates by customer and is not interchangeable with a month-level currency lookup.

views.description: Canonical monthly FX rates to USD from currency table, one row per year+month, exposing to_us and a canonical month identifier. Use when normalizing amounts to USD or when joining by year/month. | Use for: Converting local amounts to USD using monthly FX; Joining sales or costs aggregated by month to FX rates
